    32	
    33	## 1. The decision in one page
    34	
    35	Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
    36	of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.
    37	
    38	**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):
    39	
    40	1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
    41	   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
    42	2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets an approved grant
    43	   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h, ⚠️ R2.9 #3) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
    44	3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.
    45	
    46	| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
    47	|---|---|
    48	| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
    49	| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |
    50	| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). From phase 2 you push and open PRs yourself and confirm each cloud CLI call (layer 2, OD34). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
    51	| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |
    52	
    53	**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**
    54	
    55	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
    56	  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
    57	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
    58	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
    59	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
    60	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
    61	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
    62	  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
    63	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
    64	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
    65	  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
    66	  laptops it rests on policy, training and managed deny rules for `gh pr review` (OD25), which
    67	  are hygiene: another form of the same call is not matched (📖 R9.4.1). An agent could still
    68	  approve through its engineer's login. A review does not show whether it came from the web or
    69	  the API (📖 R9.1.10); the approval-gate app only flags suspicious approvals (OD27). And "named"
    70	  means a GitHub account that a register maps to a person: SAML SSO needs Enterprise Cloud
    71	  (📖 R9.1.2), so on Team the mapping is a process (layer 1, OD25).
    72	- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
    73	  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
    74	  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). GitHub accepts an
    75	  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so the approval-gate app enforces the rest (OD27,
    76	  [design]): an on-call approval counts for another team's file only if the PR links an open
    77	  incident and the approver is on shift. A label alone grants nothing, since anyone with Triage
    78	  can apply it (📖 R9.1.9). Because on-call approvers only
    79	  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
    80	  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
    81	- **One approver for most high-risk changes.** L3 changes in deployable code (IAM, stateful
    82	  deletes, network) get one approver, like L2, from the owners of the path (the stack's owners for
    83	  L3 content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at the prod preview (OD2,
    84	  OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off for speed. The
    85	  exception is the **process paths** (workflows, CODEOWNERS, agent config, catalogue, SCP and IAM
    86	  stacks, risk stop): two L3 owner team members, enforced by the approval-gate app (OD26). They change
    87	  rarely, are never urgent at night, and one compromised login must not be enough to change them.
    88	- **k0s and Firebase are weaker:** no prod preview or risk stop, no break-glass when Actions is
    89	  down (G1, G2), and their deploy credentials are stored in GitHub (OD1). For k0s, the interim
    90	  controls of OD24 (a namespaced, time-limited deploy token and the Kubernetes API audit log) rely
    91	  on `extraArgs`, which is "outside k0s support" (📖 R9.3.1).
    92	- **New dependencies on two GitHub Apps** (required check, CI agent): if the required-check app is
    93	  down, every merge to `main` is blocked, incident PRs included; that counts as "pipeline
    94	  unavailable" for JIT. The required-check app now enforces OD26 and OD27 too, so it is a hard
    95	  phase-1 prerequisite (rollout); its decision logic is an example (E12), its keys and hosting are
    96	  open (G19). It is also the longest phase-1 item (10–15 person-days, ⚠️ estimate, OD35).
    97	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
    98	  business associate, as the brief implies.
    99	
   100	**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):
   101	
   102	1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
   103	   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
   104	2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
   105	3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
   106	4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.
   107	
   108	### Roles
   109	
   110	| Role | Rule |
   111	|---|---|
   112	| Author (engineer + their agent) | Never approves own change; GitHub blocks PR authors from approving (📖 R3.3.1). |
   113	| Approver | Always an engineer, never an agent (owner rule, OD5). Named in CODEOWNERS; ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3); for an app-opened PR, ≠ the person who triggered it (⚠️ R3.3.4, layer 5). Their GitHub account is in the login register (OD25). Process paths need two (OD26). |
   114	| Incident responder | Engineer who diagnoses and writes the fix or the JIT request. Never the on-call approver of the same shift (OD7). |
   115	| On-call approver | Engineer on the on-call schedule, primary + backup, 24/7; wait ≤ 15 min (S7). Approves another team's file only for a PR linked to an open incident while on shift, checked by the approval-gate app (OD27). While on call they only approve: they write no fix and file no JIT request, so the approver is always distinct from the author (OD7). The primary approves; the backup replaces an unavailable primary (OD2). No platform-team membership is required; all engineers follow one agreed approval procedure (OD2). |
   116	| Data owner [design] | Named per tenant; co-approves real-data reads, or reviews a night-time read the next working day (layer 6). |
   117	| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1); owns policies and metrics; not the only approver. |
   118	| L3 owner team | Owns the process-defining L3 paths and the SCP stack (layer 3); composition open (G17). |

   121	
   122	## Layer 1 — Identity and access
   123	
   124	**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
   125	written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
   126	to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.
   127	
   128	**On Papaya's stack**
   129	
   130	- **The engineer's access is the agent's access.** The agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and
   131	  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse
   132	  detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate
   133	  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
   134	  holds.
   135	- **Process rules** that follow from this:
   136	  - the JIT terminal runs no agent, though the grant is reachable from the same laptop (owner
   137	    accepted as a process control, D2);
   138	  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles (D2; `--restricted` per D3,
   139	    research 6.9.4 Q2);
   140	  - the real-data terminal runs no agent when the store holds PHI [design], same weakness as D2;
   141	  - an agent never approves PRs: an owner rule (OD5), enforced on laptops by policy, training and
   142	    managed deny rules for `Bash(gh pr review *)` and `Bash(gh api *reviews*)` plus
   143	    `Read(~/.config/gh/**)` from phase 1 (OD25; valid patterns, not a boundary, 📖 R9.4.1).
   144	    GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
   145	    excerpt read names "approving Claude's own pull request" (📖 R6.3.3); whether approving
   146	    someone else's PR is blocked is unverified (⚠️), and the list
   147	    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no
   148	    documented meaning, R3.5.6).
   149	- **IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1) [design names]:
   150	  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim
   151	    stores; 1 h session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). Some "metadata" reads (mostly ⚠️) return configuration or
   152	    secrets, so `Resource: "*"` only for a reviewed action list (examples E6, findings 11, 12). Until a service's logs are redacted at source
   153	    and masked (layer 6, OD28), it gets that service's metrics only. Lambda configuration can hold secrets resolved by
   154	    Serverless in plain text (⚠️ R4.4.7), so configuration reads are allowed per service only after
   155	    its secrets move to runtime resolution (⚠️ R4.6 #7). Cost: until then the agent reads
   156	    timeout/memory from the IaC code;
   157	  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad, non-prod accounts only;
   158	  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: assigned only by the JIT flow's receiver (layer 7, OD33) after its
   159	    pre-grant check (examples E16), on the documented APIs `CreateAccountAssignment` /
   160	    `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2). A partner product or the TEAM sample (📖 R2.4.1,
   161	    R2.4.1b) can replace the receiver only if it enforces the same checks before the grant;
   162	  - no standing prod-write permission set.
   163	- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
   164	  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
   165	    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
   166	    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
   167	  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
   168	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
   169	    JIT roles. The Serverless prod deploy role is a separate role and is not exempt: it only passes
   170	    the `deploymentRole` (examples finding 13). This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
   171	    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (key 📖 R4.4.5; need ⚠️ R4.6 #3);
   172	  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:UserId` (📖 R2.4.4); deny changes to any trail
   173	    in prod accounts, since member accounts cannot touch the organization trail anyway (📖 R2.6.2;
   174	    examples findings 10, 15);
   175	  - exempt role names are protected: only the IAM stack's deploy role may create or change such
   176	    roles (OD19), and from phase 1 that is a role of its own (OD22): the IAM stack deploys from a
   177	    separate GitHub environment, `production-iam`, whose OIDC subject only that role trusts. So
   178	    code running in a domain stack's deploy job cannot obtain it. Domain deploy roles (and the
   179	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole` of each Serverless stack) may create or change only `svc-*`
   180	    roles, and only with a fixed permissions boundary attached that they cannot remove or edit
   181	    (pattern 📖 R9.2.1; role action list ⚠️; examples E4b). The boundary denies `iam:*` and
   182	    root sessions. Cost: Lambda and ECS roles that read claim data (`app-claims-*`) live in the
   183	    IAM stack and are referenced by ARN (examples finding 16);
   184	  - deny every action of `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` in the prod OU (OD23). Organizations
   185	    creates this role with "full administrative permissions" in each account it creates, trusted
   186	    by the management account (📖 R9.2.4); SCPs cover it as any other member-account role
   187	    (📖 R9.2.6, inference). Using it in an emergency needs an SCP change, an L3 path.
   188	  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
   189	    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path, held by the L3 owner team only, not co-owned by the on-call group; OD13).
   190	- **GitHub identity (OD25).** An approval proves a GitHub account; Compliance needs a named person
   191	  [design unless marked]:
   192	  - the organization requires two-factor authentication (📖 R9.1.1; the page names no plan, so
   193	    ⚠️ check the setting in Papaya's Team organization);
   194	  - a login register maps every member's GitHub login to an employee, fed by HR joiners and
   195	    leavers; a leaver is removed from the organization on the last day; reviewed quarterly (C-03);
   196	  - outside collaborators get no write access to the monorepo; classic personal access tokens are
   197	    restricted and fine-grained tokens need approval and a maximum lifetime (📖 R9.1.12; plan not
   198	    stated ⚠️);
   199	  - SAML SSO, which would tie the login to the identity provider, needs Enterprise Cloud
   200	    (📖 R9.1.2); see "GitHub plan" in layer 3.
   201	- **Who administers the administrators (OD23).** Whoever administers IAM Identity Center can
   202	  assign themselves any permission set, so "no standing prod write" holds only if that power is
   203	  itself controlled [design unless marked]:
   204	  - permission sets and account assignments are code in an identity stack (an L3 path, L3 owner

388	## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level
389	
390	**Principle.** The level is set by the damage a change can do. One default path above non-prod: a
391	reviewed PR applied by the pipeline, with the JIT fallback (layer 7) as the only other write path.
392	The approver reviews the code change that will be applied. By default a prod change needs two
393	people: one who makes it and one who approves it; the on-call backup only replaces an unavailable
394	primary (OD2). Higher risk narrows **who** may approve (the owners of that path), not how many, with
395	two exceptions: a process path needs two L3 owner team members (OD26), and a PR that touches files of
396	several teams needs an owner of each, except in an incident (OD27). Separately, any prod diff that looks risky stops the deploy, whatever its level; that adds a
397	second approval by an owner of the same stack, which keeps it to two people (OD8). Confirmed by the owner

836	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
837	
838	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
839	Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
840	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
841	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
842	tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
843	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).
844	
845	**On Papaya's stack**
846	
847	- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
848	  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role from
849	    phase 1 (existing broad read roles are removed) and the SCP from phase 2
850	    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
851	    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
852	  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
853	  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
854	    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
855	  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
856	    Redaction lives in application code, so one approved PR that logs a whole event would put
857	    PHI in a log group the agent reads. A second layer outside the code (OD28) [design]:
858	    - a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy on every log group `ProdReadMetadata` reads, set
859	      **before** the group is opened, because masking applies at ingestion only; masked data is
860	      hidden "at all egress points, including CloudWatch Logs Insights" (📖 R9.2.7);
861	    - custom identifiers keyed on field names (national ID, HKID, bank account, diagnosis,
862	      insured name; examples E14), because AWS has no managed identifier for Vietnam, Thailand
863	      or Hong Kong (📖 R9.2.8); at most 10, each regex ≤ 200 characters (📖 R9.2.9);
864	    - no agent-usable role holds `logs:Unmask`, and none gets `CloudWatchLogsFullAccess`, which
865	      includes it (📖 R9.2.7; E6 test);
866	    - a required SAST rule against logging whole events or payload objects in the claims
867	      services' handlers (S10; product open, G4); a log-level change already stops at the risk
868	      stop (`logging` property), because debug output can carry PHI.
869	    Limit: field-name masking catches structured logs, not free text in a message. It is a second
870	    layer; code review and the SAST rule remain the first. Cost: $0.12 per GB scanned
871	    (📖 R9.2.10) and masked values while debugging.
872	- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
873	  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. At night the data owner is not on call: the
874	  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day. This
875	  applies to non-PHI and PHI alike; for PHI the reader is still a human without an agent. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
876	  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
877	  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent (process rule, layer 1); the agent gets a
878	    redacted summary. This
879	    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
880	    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
881	  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9). Claim
882	    tables mix health, ID and bank data (research 1.11.4 L2), so a store that holds PHI is treated as
883	    PHI unless the agent reads a view or extract without PHI [design].
884	- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
885	  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
886	  1.11.4 L6).
887	- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default (sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, layer 2); the auto-mode
888	  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions and 5.7 % of 1,000 synthetic exfiltration
889	  attempts (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path

890	  (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no WebFetch, likely no edit tools (layer 2), and runs outside
891	  the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
892	  commands (layer 2), including the SSO token cache; "no standing write, no PHI read" limits what
893	  the token opens, except during a JIT or data-read window (layer 2 mitigations). Shared knowledge
894	  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is exempt from the protected-path rules unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
895	- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
896	  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed

900	  not part of the free loop.

902	  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).

904	  abroad is a transfer (📖 R5.4.5); agent flows, including employee names in logs and transcripts,

1033	## Layer 8 — Governance and rollout
1034	
1035	**Principle.** Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date. Policies are files changed by
1036	PR. Access is never removed before its replacement works. Controls are tested against realistic
1037	attacks.
1038	
1039	**On Papaya's stack**
1040	
1041	- **Owners:** DevSecOps (framework, managed settings, catalogue, metrics); a platform team or named
1042	  engineers (deploy workflows, rulesets, pipelines; whether Papaya has a platform team is unknown ⚠️); Compliance (evidence review, supplier register, Statement of
1043	  Applicability); engineering leads (decide CODEOWNERS content; changes to it are approved by the L3 owner team); engineering management (on-call schedule).
1044	- **Policy as code:** catalogue, SCPs, trust policies, CODEOWNERS and workflows are files under
1045	  CODEOWNERS. Settings that live outside files are kept as an expected copy in git and compared with
1046	  the live state: GitHub settings (⚠️ R3.6 #1; G8) and Claude managed settings, which are edited in
1047	  the admin console (📖 R1.1.5; comparison method in layer 2). Few GitHub admins and Claude org
1048	  Owners, reviewed quarterly.
1049	- **Metrics:** S1–S11 exactly as in framing §5; this framework adds the JIT metrics (layer 7) and the
1050	  prompt metrics (layer 2). S2 and S5 have caveats (OD1; layer 2).
1051	- **Rollout** (≈ 90 days, GĐ-12 unconfirmed): [`03-rollout-plan.md`](03-rollout-plan.md), moved
1052	  there with its items unchanged except syncs with the examples' findings (trail deny, allowlist,
1053	  phase-2 version floor), and expanded with owners and checks [design]. Order (framing Q8): (1) remove long-lived CI credentials, (2) narrow standing prod
1054	  access, (3) MCP/plugin catalogue; the on-call approver list before or with (2). Phase 1 (0–30 days)
1055	  makes the PR the default prod write path, with seven hard prerequisites before standing prod write is
1056	  removed; phase 2 (30–60) adds SCPs, the rest of the managed baseline and automated
1057	  reconciliation; phase 3 (60–90) tests and reviews. The phase-1 load is the main rollout risk: a
1058	  rough estimate (⚠️) is 75–110 person-days, so the rollout plan names a minimum safe phase 1 for 2
1059	  DevSecOps people and one platform engineer over about 45 days, and a degraded mode if the
1060	  approval-gate app is late (OD35).
1061	
1062	- **Exceptions:** a ticket with owner, reason and expiry.
1063	- **Standards mapping:** ISO 27001:2022 Annex A (IDs recalled, ⚠️ R5.1), HIPAA Security Rule
1064	  (📖 R5.2) and Vietnam law (📖 R5.4) are mapped per control area in the
1065	  [compliance register](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference), with every caveat. "A named human approves"
1066	  is Papaya's chosen way to meet these controls, not a literal requirement (⚠️ R5.7 #1).
1067	- **Out of scope:** security of the production AI agents (A7a); noted as a follow-up.
1068	
1069	**Audit evidence.** Git history of policy files, monthly metrics, 90-day review minutes, the exception register and planted-injection reports; standards: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference).
1070	
1071	**Cost / value.** Steady, small overhead for DevSecOps and the owners of deploy workflows. Compliance gets a managed system
1072	with owners and review dates.

836	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
837	
838	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
839	Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
840	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
841	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
842	tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
843	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).
844

846

1035	**Principle.** Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date. Policies are files changed by
1036	PR. Access is never removed before its replacement works. Controls are tested against realistic
1037	attacks.

1	# Engineer guide: working with Claude Code at Papaya
     2	
     3	> Status: a summary of the approved framework; it adds no rule · Updated: 2026-11-09 · Builds on
     4	> [`01-framework.md`](01-framework.md)
     5	
     6	This page answers one question: **what changes in my working day?** Each section says what you do,
     7	who approves, and how long it takes. The rules and their sources are in the framework layer linked
     8	from each section; if this page and the framework differ, the framework wins. Times are targets from
     9	the success criteria (S-n) or estimates marked ⚠️.
    10	
    11	## The short version
    12	
    13	- **Non-prod is yours.** Build, deploy and debug in non-prod with the agent, with no new approval (S4),
    14	  once a store has been scanned for real data (until then it follows the real-data rule, section 5).
    15	- **Prod reads are metrics and metadata.** No standing prod write for anyone, you included.
    16	- **Every prod change is a pull request.** One code owner who is not you approves; CI applies it.
    17	- **In an incident the path is the same, with faster people:** an on-call approver, 24/7.
    18	- **Real customer data, new tools and break-glass need a request.** Each has a named approver and a time limit.
    19	
    20	## 1. Daily development (non-prod)
    21	
    22	- **What you do:** use Claude Code as you do today, with non-prod roles. Manual permission mode is the
    23	  default; you may switch to auto mode (D1). Commands that run inside the sandbox run without a prompt
    24	  (phase 2, OD12).
    25	- **Approval:** none (risk level L1).
    26	- **What is different:** the organisation's managed settings apply to everyone; bypass mode is
    27	  removed; plugins and MCP servers come from the catalogue only (section 6). From phase 2 the sandbox
    28	  hides credentials and blocks Unix sockets, so `git push`, `gh`, Docker and private-registry `npm ci` fail inside it: run
    29	  them yourself at the `!` prompt. Using `--restricted` is recommended (D3).
    30	- **Workarounds (OD34):** ask the agent to write the PR text to a file, then run `git push` and
    31	  `gh pr create --body-file <file>` at the `!` prompt; run Docker-based tests in CI on the PR;
    32	  private packages install with the read-only registry token set up for you. For prod questions use
    33	  metrics and masked logs through `ProdReadMetadata` (section 4) before asking for real data (section 5).
    34	- **From phase 2 you will also notice** (layer 2, examples E8): each `aws`, `pulumi` or `serverless`
    35	  call asks you first, in auto mode too; each WebFetch asks; your own and the project's permission
    36	  rules are ignored, so prompts may rise; sign-in is locked to Papaya's organisation (API-key sessions
    37	  are refused) and the minimum Claude Code version rises; on macOS, servers on localhost fail inside
    38	  the sandbox; native Windows is not supported (use WSL2).
    39	- **Layer:** [2](01-framework.md#layer-2--agent-runtime-controls).
    40	
    41	## 2. Reading prod
    42	
    43	- **What you do:** with `ProdReadMetadata` (1-hour session) you and your agent read metrics, metadata
    44	  and logs that are redacted at source and masked by a data protection policy (OD28): identifiers
    45	  such as national IDs, bank accounts and diagnoses show as masked values. Lambda configuration is readable per service once its secrets
    46	  are resolved at runtime; until then, read timeout and memory from the IaC code.
    47	- **Approval:** none (L0).
    48	- **Cost to know:** in the first months, raw logs of services not yet redacted are not readable
    49	  without a data-read request (section 5). This is the largest cost of the transition.
    50	- **Remember:** the agent uses **your** AWS SSO session, so it can do whatever you can (layer 1). Keep
    51	  the portal session short.
    52	- **Layer:** [1](01-framework.md#layer-1--identity-and-access).
    53	
    54	## 3. Shipping a prod change
    55	
    56	1. Write the change as code (Pulumi, `serverless.yml`, Kubernetes manifests) and preview it on non-prod.
    57	2. Push the branch and open a pull request. The PR runs secret scanning, dependency checks and SAST
    58	   (S10), and previews non-prod only.
    59	3. One code owner of the changed files approves. You cannot approve your own PR, and the approver may
    60	   not be the last person who pushed. An agent never approves a PR (OD5). Managed settings deny `gh pr review` for agents, but
    61	   that is hygiene only: another form of the same call gets past it, so the approval-gate check
    62	   flags approvals that look automated rather than blocking them (OD25).
    63	   - Domain code and stacks: your domain team. Members of the on-call group are co-owners, but
    64	     their approval counts for another team's files only on an incident PR while they are on shift;
    65	     the approval-gate check enforces it (OD27). A PR that touches several teams' files needs an
    66	     owner of each.
    67	   - Process files (`.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/`, the catalogue, the SCP and IAM stacks,
    68	     `tools/risk-stop/`, `tools/ci/`, `oncall/`): **two** members of the L3 owner team (OD26,
    69	     OD32). A night fix that needs an IAM change goes through JIT.
    70	   - Clicking "Update branch" after someone else's merge keeps your approvals as long as your own
    71	     changes are the same; a push that changes them needs a new approval (OD31).
    72	4. Merge (squash only). The deploy job previews prod and applies the change.
    73	5. **If the deploy stops at the risk stop** (stateful replace or delete, IAM, network, a policy
    74	   finding): open a second PR that adds only `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<stopped commit>.yaml` with the
    75	   hash from the job summary. By default the first approver approves it; if they are unavailable,
    76	   another owner of the stack does, which is recorded as a deviation (OD13, OD11). Merging it deploys
    77	   if the new prod preview has the same hash. While the stack is stopped, later merges to it stop too.
    78	
    79	- **Time:** same working day from PR to prod; approval wait ≤ 1 hour in working hours (S4 targets).
    80	- **What CI does differently (OD22):** npm install scripts do not run in preview and deploy jobs;
    81	  if a package needs its script, ask the L3 owner team to add it to `tools/ci/allowed-install-scripts.txt`.
    82	  A stack may create IAM roles for its own services only as `svc-*` roles with the standard
    83	  permissions boundary; roles that read claim data (`app-claims-*`) are created in the IAM stack
    84	  and referenced by ARN. PRs that touch infrastructure code also get an automated agent review,
    85	  which is advice, not an approval.
    86	- **Layer:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level); diagram
    87	  [`01-change-workflow`](../diagrams/01-change-workflow.svg).
    88	
    89	- **Other platforms (OD36, OD40):** mobile releases and over-the-air updates go through the same PR;
    90	  the CI publishes to the `production` EAS channel, and nobody runs `eas update` against it from a
    91	  laptop (your Expo role cannot). GCP prod access for a person is a Privileged Access Manager
    92	  request approved by the on-call approver, never a standing role; k0s access for people is
    93	  read-only through single sign-on once OIDC is in place.
    94	
    95	## 3a. Database changes and data fixes
    96	
    97	- **Schema and metadata:** write the migration (or GraphQL-engine metadata change) as a file under
    98	  `db/<service>/`, open a PR, get your domain owner's approval as for code. After merge the `sql`
    99	  deploy job applies it with its own database role; nobody, you included, holds database
   100	  credentials (OD29, ADR-0011).
   101	- **Data fix** (a stuck claim, a payout to retry): a file `db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`
   102	  for one tenant, with a `-- expected_rows: N` header. It needs a code owner **and** a different
   103	  person from that tenant's data owners (L3-data-write). The job rolls it back if the row count
   104	  differs, and its summary shows counts only.
   105	- **Expect a stop** for `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, column type changes, `DELETE`/`UPDATE` without a
   106	  `WHERE`, grants and row-level security, and every metadata change: open the
   107	  `deploy-approvals/` PR as in step 5 above. Prefer expand/contract migrations.
   108	- **In an incident:** the same path; the on-call approver may stand in for the data owner, who
   109	  reviews it the next working day.
   110	- **Layer:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level).
   111	
   112	## 4. An incident at 2 a.m.
   113	
   114	You are the **incident responder**. The **on-call approver** only approves; they never write the fix (OD7).
   115	
   116	1. Start an incident-analysis session with read-only roles, in an empty scratch directory outside
   117	   the repository: `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"` (no WebFetch; Bash can still reach
   118	   the network). Read metrics and redacted logs.
   119	2. Open (or find) the incident issue in Linear. Make the fix in a normal session, preview on
   120	   non-prod, and open a PR labelled `incident` that links the issue: the on-call approval counts
   121	   only while the issue is open and the approver is on shift (OD27).
   122	3. Call the on-call approver (phone in phase 1; routed alerts from phase 2). They review and approve.
   123	   If they find a problem, you push the fix and they approve again.
   124	4. Merge; the deploy job applies the change. If it stops at the risk stop, the approval PR it
   125	   needs (`deploy-approvals/<stack>/`) goes the same way: label it `incident` and link the same
   126	   open issue, or the approval-gate check does not count the on-call approval on it either.
   127	
   128	- **Time:** target ≤ 15 min waiting for approval (S7); 11–46 min from decision to apply is an
   129	  estimate (⚠️), measured first during rollout against a 30-minute target.
   130	- **Blockers to know:** a risky change already waiting on `main` blocks your fix for that stack until
   131	  it is approved or reverted; at night, process files (workflows, `CLAUDE.md`, catalogue) wait for the
   132	  L3 owner team, or the JIT fallback applies.
   133	- **Only if the PR path cannot be used** (GitHub Actions down, broken pipeline, an operation not in
   134	  IaC): end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then open a JIT request issue in Linear from
   135	  its template (outside GitHub), with the exact commands; it is the record of the request (OD30). The on-call approver approves before the grant by
   136	  moving the issue to "Approved"; the grant then arrives automatically, and is refused if you
   137	  approved it yourself, the approver is not on shift or the incident is closed (OD33).
   138	  You get `InfraOperator-<service>` (1-hour role session; the real window can approach 2 h) and type
   139	  the commands yourself, in a terminal **without an agent**. Afterwards your commands are compared
   140	  with CloudTrail (by hand in phase 1, by a job from phase 2), and you open a PR that codifies the change.
   141	- **Layers:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level),
   142	  [7](01-framework.md#layer-7--observability-audit-incident-response-and-break-glass); diagram
   143	  [`03-incident-lane`](../diagrams/03-incident-lane.svg).
   144	
   145	## 5. Reading real customer data
   146	
   147	- **What you do:** end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then open a data-read request issue
   148	  in Linear from its template, with one tenant, purpose, store, time window and the agreement that
   149	  covers it (OD30). You get a data-read role for 1 hour.
   150	  After reading one tenant's data, do not post to shared places without review.
   151	- **Approval:** an approver who is not you, plus the data owner. At night the on-call approver
   152	  approves alone, and the data owner reviews it the next working day.
   153	- **PHI (medical records):** you read it yourself, in a terminal **without an agent**; give the agent
   154	  only a redacted summary. A store that holds PHI counts as PHI unless the agent reads a view without
   155	  it. Partner-uploaded claim documents never go into an agent session raw: reproduce with synthetic
   156	  documents, or de-identify them first.
   157	- **Non-prod** should hold no real data; a store not yet scanned follows this section's rule.
   158	- **Layer:** [6](01-framework.md#layer-6--data-protection-and-prompt-injection-defence).
   159	
   160	## 6. Adding a plugin or MCP server
   161	
   162	- **What you do:** open a request with what the tool reads, where it sends data and which write
   163	  tools it needs. A local MCP server is admitted only as a container image pinned by digest or as
   164	  code inside a pinned plugin, not as `npx -y <package>` (OD26). Keep your GitHub CLI token in the
   165	  system credential store (`gh auth status` shows where it is). A catalogue entry is added by a PR with a review record (examples
   166	  [`reviews/`](../examples/claude/marketplace/reviews/)).
   167	- **Approval:** two members of the L3 owner team (the catalogue is a process path, OD26).
   168	- **Time:** decided within 5 working days (S6).
   169	- **Not allowed:** installing a plugin or MCP server outside the catalogue, or sideloading one with
   170	  command-line flags.
   171	- **Layer:** [4](01-framework.md#layer-4--supply-chain-for-mcp-servers-and-plugins).
   172	
   173	## 7. When you are the on-call approver
   174	
   175	- You are on a named 24/7 schedule: a primary and a backup. The primary approves; the backup steps in
   176	  only if the primary is unavailable (OD2).
   177	- While on call you **only approve**: you do not write fixes or request JIT grants (OD7). A night
   178	  incident therefore needs two people awake: the responder and you.
   179	- Target: approve within 15 minutes (S7). Approve JIT only when the PR path cannot be used, and record
   180	  why you refuse it otherwise.
   181	- Approve another domain's PR only if it is labelled `incident`, links an open incident, and you
   182	  are on shift (OD9, OD27); the approval-gate check does not count it otherwise.
   183	- **Layers:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level),
   184	  [7](01-framework.md#layer-7--observability-audit-incident-response-and-break-glass).
   185	
   186	## 8. Shared agent knowledge
   187	
   188	`CLAUDE.md` and other agent configuration files define how the whole team works, so changes to them
   189	are approved by two members of the L3 owner team; a domain-team approval does not count (OD3, OD26). Review your agent's auto memory
   190	and delete it after a suspicious session (D3).
   191	
   192	## Where the evidence comes from
   193	
   194	You do not write separate evidence: the PR, its approvals, the deploy run and CloudTrail form the
   195	record of every prod change. Compliance's view is in
   196	[`04-compliance-mapping.md`](04-compliance-mapping.md).

## What the controls do not cover

- **Management account:** SCPs do not apply there (📖 R9.2.6), so its small named group is a
  detective control only (T22).
- **Process-only controls:** raw partner documents kept out of agent sessions (T1); no agent in the JIT
  or PHI terminal (T6, T14); agents never approve PRs on laptops (T7); tenant posting rule (T6); incident-session flags (T19). They
  rely on training and are checked by sampling, not enforced.
- **Code outside the sandbox:** hooks, plugins and local MCP servers are limited only by review before
  approval (T2, T3); excluded commands (`aws`, `pulumi`, `serverless`) only by prompts (`ask` rules from phase 2,
  in auto mode too), while the repo code they run may have been changed without a prompt (T1, T10).
- **Laptops without MDM:** server-managed settings can be skipped (T2–T4; G11). The IAM and merge-gate
  boundaries still hold.
- **k0s, GCP and Firebase:** mechanisms designed (OD36) but untested and mostly phase 2 (G1–G3); no
  risk stop, no break-glass; a leaked k0s deploy token is limited and logged (OD24), a leaked
  Firebase key is not detected. Mobile updates: see T25.
- **Phase 1 window:** until phase 2 there is no sandbox, only one credential deny rule (`Read(~/.aws/**)`, OD21), no
  `allowManagedHooksOnly`, no `allowedProviders`, no SCPs, no audit-log alerts and no policy checks
  (T1, T3–T5, T10, T12–T14, T17). Standing prod write stays until its prerequisites are in place ([rollout plan](03-rollout-plan.md#hard-prerequisites-before-standing-prod-write-is-removed-item-116)).

# Problem → control map

> Status: approved by the owner 2026-11-09 · Updated: 2026-11-09 · Source of the problems:
> `work/01-problem-framing.md` §1 (P = sentences of the brief, A = facts of its Appendix A)

## How to read this

One row per problem from the framing. **Controls** name the framework layer (L1–L8; "risk-level L3" means the change level of layer 3), ADR or threat
(T*n*, [`05-threat-model.md`](05-threat-model.md)) that answers it. **Evidence** is what shows the control
works. Codes: S*n* success criteria and GĐ-*n* assumptions of the framing, G*n* framework gaps,
OD*n* owner decisions, D1–D3 owner decisions in research 6.6, "Options §n" sections of
`work/03-options.md`. **Coverage**:

- **Covered:** the core of the problem is closed by a control enforced outside the agent (IAM,
  GitHub, CI). What stays open is listed as **Residual**; a date (end of phase 1, phase 2) says when
  the control is in place.
- **Partial:** the control is process only, or the core of the problem is still open. Laptop-side
  settings count as process, since they can be skipped without MDM (ADR-0007).
- **Gap:** the core of the problem has no control in this framework; partial mitigations may be
  listed, and the open part is marked **none** with the reason.
- **Out of scope:** excluded by the framing (§1.4).

Markers follow the framework legend (📖, ⚠️, [design]). `[map finding, not in framework gaps]` marks an
open point this map found that the framework's gap list (G1–G20) does not yet contain; claims about tools are cited in the framework
and ADRs, so this table points there rather than repeating citations.

# ADR-0003: The merge to `main` is the approval gate: two people, code owners, on-call co-ownership

- **Status:** Accepted; superseded in part by [ADR-0012](0012-approval-integrity-checked-by-the-gate-app.md)
  (which approvals count, two approvers on process paths, on-call approvals only in an incident)
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-5, GĐ-8, GĐ-11; OD2, OD5, OD7, OD9, OD10, OD13)
- **Scope:** GitHub monorepo rulesets, CODEOWNERS, `production` environment, on-call schedule

## 1. Context

Papaya is assumed to be on GitHub Team (GĐ-5), where environment required reviewers do not exist for
private repositories (📖 R3.1.2), so the approval must happen before the deploy job. Incidents need an
approver within 15 minutes, 24/7 (S7), and code-owner review requires an approval from an owner of the files (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7;
per-file behaviour ⚠️).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Upgrade to Enterprise for environment reviewers | Approval sits next to the deploy | Cost; not assumed (GĐ-5) |
| B. Merge to `main` as the gate; `production` limited to `main` | Works on Team; the approver sees the code that will be applied | Nobody sees the prod diff before apply (partly handled by ADR-0004) |
| C. More approvers for high-risk changes | More eyes | Slower; the owner wants two people per change |

## 3. Decision

Option B. Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5); branch up to date, since there is no merge queue
(⚠️ R4.6 #1). `production` accepts only `main` (📖 R3.1.3).

- **Merge = deploy approval** only if the reusable deploy workflow alone references `production`,
  with no ref/SHA inputs, no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers, one
  concurrency group per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4; ⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c).
- **Two people per change:** one makes it, one approves it; the approver is always an engineer,
  never an agent (OD2, OD5). L3 changes need one approver too, who must own the path.
- **Incidents:** on-call engineers only approve; an incident responder writes the fix (OD7).
- **Night coverage:** an on-call approver group co-owns every deployable path in CODEOWNERS; one
  primary, one backup (OD9). It does not co-own process-defining paths (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS,
  agent config, catalogue) or the SCP stack, which only the L3 owner team approves (OD13); IAM-only
  stacks are deployable, so it co-owns them with the L3 owner team. *Superseded by OD32: the IAM
  stack is a process path, L3 owner team only.*
- **Agent review:** an independent agent may post an automated review; it never counts as an
  approval (GĐ-11).
- **Cross-team PRs:** one approval is enough (OD10). *Superseded by ADR-0012: each team's files need
  their own owner's approval; the on-call approval covers another team's files only in an incident (OD27).*

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** four-eyes enforced by GitHub, not by the agent; one rule for normal days and incidents.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** GitHub accepts an approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so the
  on-call group can approve another domain's PR; domain review on normal days is a process rule.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can edit the gate, logged, not prevented (⚠️ R3.2.2, R3.6 #1;
  logging 📖 R3.2.2); alerts on ruleset changes; monthly report of cross-domain approvals. An agent could approve through its engineer's login; no detection found (⚠️). The
  required-check app's hosting, key and triggers are open (⚠️ G19).
- **Next steps:** rulesets, CODEOWNERS and its validation check in phase 1; the required-check app
  before any agent workflow may open PRs; L3 owner team composition open (G17).

## 5. References

- Framework layer 3 ("Gate = merge to `main`", "Who approves at night"), layer 7 (audit alerts).
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004.
# ADR-0008: CI uses OIDC; no long-lived CI keys, with one time-boxed exception

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (framing Q8; OD1, OD6; target S2)
- **Scope:** GitHub Actions deploy workflows to AWS, GCP, k0s and Firebase

## 1. Context

CI becomes the only routine production writer (ADR-0001), so it is the main target. Repository
secrets can be read by anyone with write access (📖 R3.5.3b), which, in the single monorepo, likely includes every engineer (⚠️ assumed) and their
agent. A long-lived key there is standing prod write in disguise.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Keep stored keys, rotate them | No migration | Standing prod write for all writers |
| B. OIDC everywhere, no exception | S2 = 0 | k0s and Firebase may not support it yet (G1, G2) |
| C. OIDC for AWS and GCP; a controlled exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials | Removes most keys now | One exception to manage |

## 3. Decision

Option C.

- **AWS:** GitHub OIDC (📖 R3.4.1); the prod role trusts only the `production` environment of the
  monorepo (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4), ideally narrowed by `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
- **GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization (📖 R3.4.5b).
- **k0s/Firebase exception** (OD1, OD6): CI deploy credentials only, until it is checked whether they
  can use OIDC. Conditions [design]: a `production` environment secret, never a repository secret
  (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3); GitHub-hosted runners, because on self-hosted runners environment secrets act
  like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5); if k0s needs a self-hosted runner, it is dedicated to the
  `production` deploy and the residual risk is recorded (⚠️ G15); a single source of truth; owner, expiry, rotation.
- `GITHUB_TOKEN` default "restricted" (📖 R3.5.3); actions pinned by lockfile or full SHA (📖 R3.5.5).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** no stored AWS or GCP keys to leak (S2); every deploy credential is tied to a reviewed
  workflow on `main`.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** one-time migration; slower action updates. The exception remains until
  G1/G2 are solved.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can change or delete the environment, and a deleted
  environment comes back without protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); alerts and a settings comparison cover it.
  The GitHub Apps used for CI agents and the required check have their own keys (⚠️ G19).
  Runtime credentials inside the cluster are out of the exception (OD6).
- **Next steps:** OIDC and removal of stored keys in phase 1; k0s/Firebase credentials moved to
  environment secrets before standing prod write is removed.

## 5. References

- Framework layer 1 ("CI → AWS", "CI → GCP"), layer 5 ("Credentials").
- Related: ADR-0001.
# ADR-0010: Risk level decides who approves, not how many; non-prod needs no approval

- **Status:** Accepted; superseded in part by [ADR-0012](0012-approval-integrity-checked-by-the-gate-app.md)
  (two approvers on process paths) and extended by [ADR-0011](0011-database-changes-through-the-pipeline.md) (L3-data-write)
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-14; OD2, OD3, OD8, OD9, OD13)
- **Scope:** every change made by engineers and their agents, from non-prod to production

## 1. Context

Engineering says "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly" (brief); the need is speed. Compliance's
sentence covers production writes only (framing §3.1). A single rule for all changes either slows non-prod for
no gain or leaves high-risk prod changes with too light a review. The owner also wants every prod
change to need two people, no more by default: one who makes it and one who approves it (OD2).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Same approval for everything | Simple | Non-prod loop slowed for no gain; high-risk changes get no extra scrutiny |
| B. More approvers as risk grows (e.g. two for L3) | More eyes on dangerous changes | Breaks the two-person rule; slower incidents |
| C. Risk level narrows who may approve, plus a risk stop; non-prod free | Fast where damage is small; specialist owners where it is large | One reviewer for high-risk changes can miss things |

## 3. Decision

Option C [design levels]:

| Level | What | Approval |
|---|---|---|
| L0 | Reads: non-prod anything, prod metadata | none |
| L1 | Changes in non-prod (synthetic or masked data only, GĐ-14) | none, author only |
| L2 | Routine prod change, e.g. Lambda memory 1024 → 2048 MB | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher |
| L3 | IAM/SCP, stateful replace/delete, network, workflow and agent-config files, catalogue, advisory policy finding (full list: framework layer 5) | 1 owner of that path; *two members of the L3 owner team on process paths (ADR-0012)* |
| L3-JIT | Break-glass in an incident | on-call approver ≠ requester (ADR-0005) |
| L3-data-write | Data fix on one tenant's rows (added by ADR-0011) | code owner + a different person from that tenant's data-owner team (ADR-0012, rule R4) |
| L3-data | Real customer data read | approver ≠ requester + agreement; data-owner co-approval [design] (ADR-0009) |

`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent-configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for the
whole team (OD3). Process-defining paths and the SCP stack are owned by the L3 owner team; IAM or
stateful changes inside a domain file are approved by that stack's owners (OD8, OD13). At every level,
the risk stop applies to any deploy whose prod diff is risky (ADR-0004).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** a free non-prod loop for engineers and agents (S4); the same two-person rule for every
  prod change, incidents included (three people only by recorded deviation, OD11). Compliance gets a written rule for who may approve what.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** one approver for high-risk changes (owner's trade-off for speed);
  `CLAUDE.md` edits wait for the L3 owner team, not the domain team that edits them most.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** the free loop holds only if non-prod has no real data; a non-prod
  store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule until scanned (S11). A risky diff hidden in an L2 PR is
  caught by the risk stop, not by the level (Pulumi and Serverless stacks only;
  k0s and Firebase have none yet, G1, G2).
- **Next steps:** non-prod data scan and CODEOWNERS with the L3 path list in phase 1; composition of
  the L3 owner team is open (G17).

## 5. References

- Framework layer 3 (levels table), layer 5 (canonical L3 path list), layer 6 (non-prod).
- Related: ADR-0003, ADR-0004, ADR-0005, ADR-0009.
# ADR-0012: Approval integrity is checked by the approval-gate app: two approvals on process paths, on-call approvals only for open incidents

- **Status:** Accepted; supersedes in part ADR-0003 (domain review on normal days as a process rule; one approval for cross-team PRs, OD10) and ADR-0010 (one approver for L3 process paths)
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission, after the independent review (`work/07-review.md`; OD26, OD27)
- **Scope:** pull requests to `main` of the monorepo; the `approval-gate` required check

## 1. Context

ADR-0003 made the merge to `main` the approval gate, with an on-call group that co-owns every
deployable path, so that one primary can approve any fix at night. GitHub accepts an approval from
any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve any domain's PR, and the
`incident` label that was meant to limit this can be applied by anyone with Triage (📖 R9.1.9).
ADR-0010 kept one approver for every level. The review also found that a compromised plugin or
local MCP server runs on every laptop and could give an attacker many GitHub logins at once
(threat T23), so a single approval on the files that define the process is one stolen login away.
A path-scoped reviewer rule was not found for GitHub Team (📖 R9.1.15), and the ruleset's approval
count is repository-wide.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Keep process rules and the monthly report | No new logic | The label is free to apply; the report misses labelled PRs; one login changes the process |
| B. Raise the ruleset to two approvals for every PR | Built into GitHub | Doubles review for every change, against S4 and the owner's two-person rule |
| C. The approval-gate app, already required, checks the rules per file | Exact rules per path; works on Team | More logic in a custom app that every merge depends on (G19) |

## 3. Decision

Option C [design]. The app's decision logic is examples E12 (`examples/approval-gate/gate.py`):

- an approval counts only if it is on the head commit, or on an earlier commit with the same diff
  against its merge base (OD31), by a human who is not the author, the last pusher of a change to
  that diff or the person who triggered an app-opened PR (📖 R9.1.10 for the review fields);
- every changed file needs a counted approval from one of its owner teams;
- an on-call group member's approval counts for another team's file only if the PR carries the
  `incident` label, links an incident that is open when the check runs, and the approver is on
  shift (OD27);
- a file owned only by the L3 owner team (a process path, including the IAM stack since OD32) needs
  two different members of that team (OD26);
- approvals within two minutes of the last push, or at night without an incident, are flagged for
  the monthly report, not blocked.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** domain review on normal days and the two-person rule on process paths are enforced,
  not trained; the incident lane cannot be opened by a label alone; flagged approvals give a
  detection signal for rubber-stamping and stolen logins.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** process-path PRs need two L3 owner team members; a cross-team PR on a
  normal day needs an owner of each team (OD10's single approval now holds only in incidents);
  a stale schedule or incident record blocks a night approval until the backup or a domain owner
  approves; every merge depends more on the app.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** if the app is down, every merge is blocked, incident PRs included,
  and the JIT fallback applies (layer 7); its hosting, key and triggers stay open (G19); the schedule
  file is an L3 path; the monthly report lists every `incident` PR and every flagged approval.
- **Next steps:** the app becomes a hard prerequisite in phase 1, before the ruleset requires its
  check (rollout).

## 5. References

- Framework layer 3 ("L3 approvals", "Who approves at night"), layer 4 ("Pinning what every
  laptop runs"), layer 7 (on-call); threat model T7, T23.
- Related: ADR-0003, ADR-0006, ADR-0010.

# `production` environment secrets and variables (names only)

Set through the environment-secrets REST API or the repository settings UI, never as
repository secrets. Values are never stored in git. Framework layer 5, owner decisions OD1 and OD6.

| Secret name | What it is | Owner | Expiry / rotation | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `K0S_DEPLOY_KUBECONFIG` | Deploy-only kubeconfig for the prod k0s cluster | `<owner team>` | `<date>`, in the exception register | S2 exception until k0s deploys can use OIDC (G1) |
| `FIREBASE_DEPLOY_TOKEN` | Firebase Hosting deploy credential | `<owner team>` | `<date>`, in the exception register | S2 exception until Firebase deploys can use OIDC (G2) |

No AWS secret is listed: AWS is reached through OIDC (`examples/aws/oidc-trust-prod-deploy.json`;
the same trust is used by both prod deploy roles).

Optional, layer 5 [design]: put these two secrets in a separate environment `production-k0s`,
also limited to `main` and referenced only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy
jobs cannot read them.

Environment **variables** (not secret, but prod-only, so kept on the environment rather than the
repository; set through the environment-variables API): `AWS_REGION`, `PROD_PULUMI_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN`, `PROD_SERVERLESS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN`,
`PULUMI_BACKEND_URL`, `PULUMI_CLI_VERSION`, `NODE_VERSION`. They are read by
`workflows/deploy-prod.yml` only.

content.content:
switch the stop off. `CODEOWNERS` adds `/tools/risk-stop/` to the L3 owner team. Confirmed by
   the owner (OD14): it extends the canonical L3 list of framework layer 5.
2. **An approval must be bound to git history, not only to a hash** [design]. Two review rounds
   found ways for one PR to carry its own risky change and approval, or for an approval to be
   reused. Rules now: read from git objects only; file named `<stopped_commit>.yaml`, never
   edited; stopped commit and approval commit both on `main`'s first-parent history, in that
   order; the approval commit touches only `deploy-approvals/<stack>/`; the stack's directory
   and the classifier unchanged since the stopped commit; at most 7 days old.
3. **Squash-only merges** [design]: `ruleset-main.json` allows only squash, so each PR is one
   commit on `main`. Cost: PR-internal history is not kept on `main`.
4. **Deploy only the tip of `main`** [design]: people with write access can re-run a workflow run
   for up to 30 days, with the same `GITHUB_SHA` (📖 GitHub docs source,
   `content/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/re-run-workflows-and-jobs.md`, via review). An
   old deploy run re-run would roll prod back without any approval. `deploy-prod.yml` stops unless
   the run's commit is the current tip of `main`, read with `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/ref/heads/main`
   (✅ branch-only form; `commits/main` could resolve to a tag named `main`). This is a new
   condition for framework layer 3's "merge approval = deploy approval" list.
5. **Classification beyond the framework's categories** [design]: the property-name rule, the
   audit/detection category and "an unknown operation stops" go beyond layer 3's list
   (stateful replace/delete, IAM, network, policy finding).
6. **The approval hash must cover changed values**, not only resource names, or an approval for
   one IAM policy would let a different change to the same policy through; and it must leave out
   values that change on every build, or an approval never matches. ⚠️ From memory, not checked:
   Serverless puts a timestamped path in the Lambda `Code.S3Key` and a code hash in
   `AWS::Lambda::Version` logical IDs; both are left out of the hash.
7. **Fail-safe CODEOWNERS default** [design]: without it, root `package.json`, a new stack or a new
   `deploy-approvals/<stack>/` folder would be unowned, and GitHub then accepts an approval from
   any writer (📖 about code owners).
8. **Same-repository reusable workflows can use `uses: $/.github/workflows/<file>`**, which GitHub
   now recommends: it resolves to the running commit, not to the runner's workspace (📖 GitHub docs
   source, `data/reusables/actions/reusable-workflow-calling-syntax.md`; flagged by zizmor's
   `self-repository` audit). `actionlint` 1.7.12 (✅ latest release on 2026-11-09, published
   2026-03-30) does not know the syntax; `validate.sh` ignores only that message.
9. **`runner.temp` is not available in job-level `env`** (✅ caught by `actionlint`); paths use
   `$RUNNER_TEMP` inside steps.

### Step 2 (identity and access)

10. **SCP "protect the org trail" is mostly redundant** for member accounts: they cannot delete
    an organization trail or turn its logging off anyway (📖 R2.6.2). E5 instead denies changes
    to any trail inside prod accounts. The framework's layer-1 bullet is reworded in the final pass.
11. **"Metadata" reads can leak configuration, data or secrets** (⚠️ response contents from
    memory of the API references): `lambda:ListFunctions` and `ecs:DescribeTaskDefinition` return
    environment variables and cannot be limited to one resource (✅ catalogue: not resource-scoped);
    `lambda:GetFunction` also returns a code download URL; `ecs:DescribeTasks` returns container
    environment overrides; `cloudformation:DescribeStacks` returns stack outputs (it could be scoped
    per stack); `cloudformation:DescribeStackEvents` returns `ResourceProperties`, "the properties
    used to create the resource" (📖 [StackEvent](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/APIReference/API_StackEvent.html)),
    which for a function includes its environment variables (⚠️ inferred); `logs:DescribeQueries`
    returns other users' query strings. E6 leaves all of them out [design];
    `lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration` is granted per function instead.
12. **AWS's annotations are signals, not a classification of customer data**: `IsDataPlane` marks
    `cloudwatch:GetMetricData` too; `sqs:ListQueues` is not marked `IsList`; and many `IsList`
    actions return data or configuration (`s3:ListBucket` object keys, `ec2:Describe*` launch
    templates, `ssm:ListCommandInvocations` output; ✅ annotations in the catalogue, ⚠️ response
    contents from memory). The tests use an explicit allowlist for `Resource: "*"`. One entry has a
    condition: `states:ListExecutions` returns execution names, so names must not be built from
    claim data [design].
13. **Two prod deploy roles** (framework layer 1 already implies it): the SCP exempts the Pulumi
    role from the Lambda-update deny, but not the Serverless role, so `serverless deploy function`
    cannot change a function outside CloudFormation (drift). It does not stop malicious code in
    the job (Limits). `deploy-prod.yml` has one credentials step per tool, so an unset role
    variable fails instead of falling back to the other role.
14. **The claim-data deny assumes a naming convention** [design]: every legitimate reader must
    match `app-claims-*` or a `DataRead-*` permission set. Lambda execution roles behind SQS event
    sources, Step Functions execution roles and an AWS Backup role that reads the bucket would be
    denied otherwise (only service-linked roles are outside SCPs, 📖 R2.3.2). Phase-2 prerequisite:
    inventory the real callers of these actions (CloudTrail, IAM last-accessed data) and add them
    before the SCP is attached.
15. **The trail deny blocks every principal in prod accounts**, including deploy roles and
    `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`: a member-account trail can only be changed after a temporary
    change to the SCP (an L3 path), or an exempt audit role would have to be added [design].
16. **Exempt role names must be protected** (OD19): the exemptions are name patterns, so anyone in
    a prod account who could create or re-trust a role named `app-claims-*` or `cfn-deployment-*`
    would bypass both denies. E5 lets only `github-prod-deploy-iam` change those roles: the IAM
    stack's own role, reachable only from the `production-iam` environment (OD22, E4, E4b). Before
    OD22 the exempt principal was the shared `github-prod-deploy-pulumi` role, which every Pulumi
    stack and any job of the deploy workflow could obtain (OD20).
    - **Residual risks:** a principal that may pass an `app-claims-*` role could create a new
      function with it (`lambda:CreateFunction` is not denied), and one that may pass
      `cfn-deployment-*` to CloudFormation could change any function through a template;
      `iam:PassRole` is left out on purpose because the Serverless role must pass
      `cfn-deployment-*`. An `InfraOperator-*` grant may change an `app-claims` function's code
      and so read claim data indirectly (accepted with break-glass, ADR-0005; JIT reconciliation
      in layer 7 is the control).
    - **Constraints and prerequisites (phase 2):** Serverless services cannot create their own
      `app-claims-*` execution roles (CloudFormation runs as `cfn-deployment-*`, not exempt); those
      roles live in the Pulumi IAM stack and are referenced by ARN. The protected roles must exist
      before the SCP is attached, and if `github-prod-deploy-iam`'s own trust breaks (e.g. the
      subject-format opt-in of E4), only an SCP change from the management account (an L3 path)
      can repair it.
17. **Gaps in the claim-data deny, under G13** (⚠️ not verified): S3 requests through access
    points may be authorised on the access-point ARN, not the bucket ARN; KMS `Decrypt` on the
    claim keys would be a second layer.
    The deny also covers `sqs:StartMessageMoveTask` (a write, ✅ catalogue), which could move claim
    messages to another queue; cost: a JIT grant cannot redrive a claims dead-letter queue.

### Step 3 (agent runtime, supply chain, policy pack)

18. **The settings schema on schemastore.org is community-maintained and lags behind**: it accepts
    unknown keys and lacks `allowedProviders` and `managedSourcesBehavior` (✅ checked). The tests
    therefore check keys by path and require a documentation source for every key it lacks.
19. **The phase-1 allowlist gives no protection for `~/.aws`, and a "read-only" wildcard rule
    can write files** (review step 3): Claude Code runs a built-in set of read-only commands
    (`cat`, `grep`, `head`, read-only `git` …) without a prompt in every mode, and the set is not
    configurable (📖 [permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#read-only-commands)).
    Leaving `cat` out of the allowlist protected nothing. Worse, `Bash(git log *)`, `Bash(git show *)`
    and `Bash(git diff *)` also match `--output=<path>`, which writes chosen content to any path
    (✅ git 2.34.1; the docs use `git log --output=<file>` as an example match). The allowlist is now
    two exact repo scripts, and those run whatever `package.json` says [limit]. Owner decision OD21
    adds two keys to phase 1: a `Read(~/.aws/**)` deny rule, which also applies to recognized
    `cat`/`head`/`tail` (📖 permissions), and `autoMode.classifyAllShell` (📖, ≥ 2.1.193), so the two
    allow rules do not skip the auto-mode classifier. Left open until the phase-2 sandbox: a command
    that reads files without naming them (`grep -r` from `~`) or a script that opens `~/.aws` itself
    is not covered by a deny rule (📖 permissions). Not chosen: `blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories`
    (📖, ≥ 2.1.257), which would also block every read outside the repository.
20. **Credential paths beyond the HIPAA template** [design]: `~/.aws` as a whole (the SSO token
    cache opens every role of the engineer, layer 2), `~/.kube`, `~/.pulumi`, `~/.config/gcloud`,
    the Firebase CLI token, `~/.docker/config.json`. `~/.config/gh` must be hidden from the sandbox
    too, not only from Claude's Read tool: sandboxed commands run without a prompt (OD12) and
    `api.github.com` is allowed, so a readable token lets the agent approve PRs as the engineer (OD5).
    This closes only the sandboxed route: an excluded CLI (`pulumi`, `serverless`) runs repository
    code outside the sandbox with full access (finding 22), so hiding credentials from the sandbox
    is hygiene, not a boundary (ADR-0007).
21. **TypeScript 7 is not yet supported by `@pulumi/pulumi`** (✅ npm peer-dependency error:
    `typescript >= 3.8.3 < 7`); the pack pins TypeScript 6.0.3.
22. **`sandbox.excludedCommands` entries match like `Bash(...)` rules** (📖
    [sandboxing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.md#run-commands-outside-the-sandbox-with-excludedcommands)):
    `aws` alone matches only `aws` with no arguments, so the first draft kept every `aws` call in the
    sandbox, where it fails (no `~/.aws`, no AWS endpoints). Entries are now `aws *`, `pulumi *`,
    `serverless *`. The docs also answer the framework's ⚠️ on matching: every command in the call
    must match; a call with `cd`, a redirect, `$(...)` or a subshell stays sandboxed; the match is on
    the text, so `/usr/local/bin/aws`, a script that calls `aws`, and `npx serverless` do not match.
    Excluded commands go through the permission flow: they prompt in Manual mode, but in auto mode
    the classifier decides (📖 sandboxing), so phase 2 also lists them as `ask` rules, which prompt
    in every mode (📖 auto-mode-config). The prompt shows the command (`pulumi preview`), not the
    repository code it runs, which a sandboxed command may have changed without a prompt.
23. **A mandatory Pulumi policy is only advisory while a value is unknown** (✅ `@pulumi/policy`
    1.21.0 `server.js` catches `UnknownValueError` and reports `advisory`). A PR-time or prod
    preview of a policy built from a resource of the same update passes; the stop comes during the
    update. Access Analyzer is the preview-time check (layer 5).
24. **The first policy pack missed the usual ways to grant admin** (review step 3): user and
    group policies, `AdministratorAccess` attached by ARN, `Role.managedPolicyArns`, and wildcards
    such as `iam:Pass*`. All are now covered and tested. Round 2: IAM also accepts `?`, so `s3:?*` and
    `*?` are full wildcards (📖 IAM Action element); covered too. Round 3: a wildcard in the service
    prefix (`*:*`, `s?:Get*`) is refused as a full wildcard (⚠️ whether IAM accepts it is unverified).
25. **The template's auto-mode `"$defaults"` pins keep the built-in rules in place** (📖
    auto-mode-config: a list without `"$defaults"` replaces the built-in rules; entries from managed
    settings cannot be removed). The first phase-2 draft dropped them, which would let a developer's
    own `hard_deny: []` discard the built-in data-exfiltration rule. Restored and tested. They are not
    a policy boundary: a developer's own `autoMode.allow` or `environment` entries still widen what the
    classifier approves ("the combination is additive, not a hard policy boundary", same page), and
    `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` does not cover `autoMode` [limit]. For prod CLIs the boundary is
    the managed `ask` rules plus layers 1 and 3.
